name: Motorcycle
title: Twin-cylinder motorcycle (700 cc)
intro: This is a 700 cc parallel-twin motorcycle. In lessons the engine case turns see-through; explode it (🧩) to see the gearbox and chain. Ask me "Why do you need to change gear?"
suggest: How does the engine turn the wheel?
Why do you need to change gear?
Why is the front brake bigger?
looksLike: motorcycle, motorbike, bike, sport bike, scooter

ride.hint: You're in the rider's seat. Drag to look around; open the throttle and change gear to see how engine rpm and speed change; tap X-ray to see the engine and gearbox under your feet.

crankcase.name: Crankcase
crankcase.info: The bottom aluminium engine case housing the crankshaft, clutch and gearbox in an oil bath for lubrication.

cylinder_block.name: Cylinder block
cylinder_block.info: Two side-by-side cylinders tilted forward 15°. Pistons reciprocate inside while coolant flows through the outer water jacket.

cylinder_head.name: Cylinder head
cylinder_head.info: Bolted atop the cylinders, holding intake and exhaust valves plus spark plugs right above the combustion chambers.

cam_cover.name: Cam cover
cam_cover.info: The top engine cover sealing the two camshafts and oil inside.

piston_r.name: Right piston
piston_r.info: Pushed down by expanding combustion gas to turn the crankshaft via the connecting rod. Shown here at top dead centre.

piston_l.name: Left piston
piston_l.info: Fires 270° after the right piston, so the two pistons never move up and down in unison.

conrod_r.name: Right connecting rod
conrod_r.info: Connects piston to crankshaft, converting up-and-down reciprocating motion into rotation.

conrod_l.name: Left connecting rod
conrod_l.info: Links the left piston to the crankshaft to convert linear push into rotation.

crankshaft.name: Crankshaft
crankshaft.info: Crank throws offset by 270° give this parallel twin an uneven firing rhythm and torque feel similar to a V-twin.

primary_gear.name: Primary gear
primary_gear.info: A 32-tooth gear on the crankshaft driving the 58-tooth clutch gear for the first speed reduction and torque boost.

camshaft_intake.name: Intake camshaft
camshaft_intake.info: Its cam lobes push the intake valves open. It spins at half the crankshaft speed to match the four-stroke cycle.

camshaft_exhaust.name: Exhaust camshaft
camshaft_exhaust.info: Pushes the exhaust valves open on time, also spinning at half the crankshaft speed.

cam_chain.name: Cam chain
cam_chain.info: Links the crankshaft to both camshafts so valve timing stays strictly in sync with the pistons.

radiator.name: Radiator
radiator.info: Front-mounted heat exchanger where oncoming air cools the hot coolant from the engine.

exhaust_headers.name: Exhaust headers
exhaust_headers.info: Two pipes routing hot exhaust gases away from the cylinder head.

clutch.name: Clutch
clutch.info: A pack of friction plates. Pulling the left lever separates them, disconnecting engine power so you can shift or stop.

clutch_cover.name: Clutch cover
clutch_cover.info: The round right-side cover sealing the clutch assembly.

mainshaft.name: Mainshaft
mainshaft.info: The gearbox input shaft driven by the clutch, carrying six drive gears.

countershaft.name: Countershaft
countershaft.info: Gearbox output shaft. Shifting selects which gear pair meshes: in 1st a small gear drives a big one for peak force; 6th is nearly one to one for top speed.

sprocket_front.name: Front sprocket
sprocket_front.info: The 15-tooth sprocket on the output shaft that pulls the drive chain.

chain.name: Drive chain
chain.info: Transfers power from the front sprocket back to the rear wheel sprocket.

sprocket_rear.name: Rear sprocket
sprocket_rear.info: The big sprocket (43 teeth) on the rear wheel. Small at the front, big at the back: another speed reduction and torque boost.

frame.name: Frame
frame.info: The main structural frame supporting the engine, front fork and swingarm.

fork.name: Front fork
fork.info: Twin suspension tubes that absorb road bumps and pivot around a 21° steering axis to steer the front wheel.

handlebar.name: Handlebar
handlebar.info: Steers the bike. Right hand controls throttle and front brake; left hand operates the clutch lever.

headlight_cowl.name: Headlight cowl
headlight_cowl.info: Front fairing around the headlight and instrument cluster.

wheel_front.name: Front wheel
wheel_front.info: The front wheel that steers the motorcycle.

disc_front_l.name: Left front disc
disc_front_l.info: Steel rotor spinning with the front wheel. Clamped by the caliper to convert speed into heat via friction.

disc_front_r.name: Right front disc
disc_front_r.info: The front wheel has two discs because weight shifts forward under braking, so the front wheel handles most of the stopping force.

calipers_front.name: Front calipers
calipers_front.info: Hydraulic pistons inside press brake pads against the front discs when you pull the brake lever.

swingarm.name: Swingarm
swingarm.info: Pivoting arm holding the rear wheel; moves up and down with the shock absorber to smooth out bumps.

wheel_rear.name: Rear wheel
wheel_rear.info: The driven wheel turned by the chain to propel the bike.

disc_rear.name: Rear disc
disc_rear.info: Rear brake rotor, smaller than the front discs because the rear wheel carries less load when braking.

caliper_rear.name: Rear caliper
caliper_rear.info: Squeezes the rear disc hydraulically when your right foot presses the brake pedal.

tank.name: Fuel tank
tank.info: Stores fuel and gives the rider a surface to grip with their knees.

seat.name: Seat
seat.info: Saddle for the rider and passenger.

side_cover_l.name: Left side cover
side_cover_l.info: Side cover under the seat housing the battery and engine control unit (ECU).

side_cover_r.name: Right side cover
side_cover_r.info: Right-hand side panel under the seat.

tail.name: Tail
tail.info: Rear tail fairing and brake light.

steps.say: Expanding gas pushes the piston down, and the connecting rod converts that up-and-down motion into crankshaft rotation.
The two crank throws sit 270° apart, so the cylinders fire in turn rather than moving together.

quiz.q: Why are the two pistons offset instead of moving up and down together?
options: So cylinders take turns firing and cancel some vibration
A 270° crank spaces out the power pulses and offsets piston inertia to reduce shaking.
To save metal
Crank offset is about firing intervals and balance, not saving material.
It's impossible to build them moving together
360° cranks do move pistons together, but they vibrate more at high speed.

steps.say: The cam chain is driven by the crankshaft to spin both camshafts, opening the intake and exhaust valves on time.

quiz.q: Why does the camshaft spin at only half the crankshaft's speed?
options: In a four-stroke cycle, each valve opens once every two crank turns
Intake, compression, power and exhaust take two crank rotations, requiring only one cam rotation.
To save fuel
The speed ratio comes from the four-stroke cycle.
It would snap if spun faster
It runs at half speed to match valve timing, not due to weak material.

drive.title: From the engine to the rear wheel

steps.say: The small gear on the crankshaft drives the big gear on the clutch, reducing speed and boosting torque first.
The clutch turns the gearbox mainshaft, which meshes with the countershaft in 1st gear.
The small front sprocket on the countershaft pulls the chain to turn the big rear sprocket for final speed reduction.

quiz.q: Why is the rear sprocket so much larger than the front sprocket?
options: To reduce speed and multiply torque so the wheel can push the bike
15 teeth driving 43 cuts speed to about a third while nearly tripling the pushing force.
Just for looks
Sprocket sizes set the final drive ratio, directly affecting acceleration and top speed.
To keep the chain from falling off
Chain tension keeps the chain on; the size difference is for torque multiplication.

steps.say: In 1st gear, a small mainshaft gear drives a large countershaft gear for maximum torque at low wheel speed.
In 6th gear, the meshing gears are nearly equal in size, spinning the rear wheel almost three times faster at the same engine rpm.

quiz.q: Why must you start from a standstill in 1st gear?
options: 1st gear multiplies torque the most to overcome standstill inertia
Starting requires peak force; once moving, you shift up to keep engine rpm reasonable.
1st gear saves the most fuel
High gears at lower engine rpm save fuel when cruising.
6th gear is too small and jams
Starting in 6th stalls the engine because there isn't enough torque multiplication.

steps.say: Pull the clutch lever before shifting to briefly disconnect engine load so the gears can engage smoothly.
Turning the handlebar pivots the front fork around the angled steering axis to steer the front wheel.
Over bumps, the rear swingarm pivots up and down against the shock absorber to keep the chassis stable.
The front wheel uses two large discs and calipers, while the rear wheel has only one small disc.

quiz.q: Why is the front brake system much larger than the rear?
options: Weight shifts forward under braking, pressing the front tyre down for maximum grip
Forward weight transfer gives the front tyre far more traction, so it handles most of the stopping force.
Because the front wheel is larger
Both wheels are similar in diameter; brake size depends on weight transfer.
The rear wheel doesn't need braking
The rear brake still helps slow and stabilise the bike, just with less force.

clutch_slip.title: Slipping clutch
clutch_slip.short: The engine revs in gear, but the bike won't go
clutch_slip.symptom: In 1st gear with throttle open, the crankshaft spins fast, yet the rear wheel barely moves. What's broken?
clutch_slip.hint: What round assembly connects the crankshaft to the gearbox mainshaft? Check whether its inner and outer parts turn together.
clutch_slip.observe: Watch the fast-spinning crankshaft and follow the drive path: which part fails to keep up first?
whys: Look at the chain—it's still intact on both sprockets. Look inside the engine: the gearbox mainshaft itself is barely turning.
Watch the pistons and crankshaft spinning rapidly—the engine has plenty of power, but it's being lost right at the gearbox entrance.
clutch_slip.cause: Worn clutch plates are slipping: the outer basket spins with the crank, but can't grip the gearbox mainshaft inside.
clutch_slip.why: Why won't the rear wheel move when the clutch slips, no matter how fast the engine spins?
clutch_slip.answer: The clutch relies on clamped friction plates to pass crankshaft power to the gearbox mainshaft. When they slip, no force enters the gearbox to reach the rear wheel.
reasons: A slipping clutch stalls the engine, stopping the rear wheel.
The clutch acts as a brake and locks the rear wheel when slipping.
